The harness refused the worker's write of `REPORT.md` in four of batch 7b's five worker passes. W's skeptic could not 
check the provenance block, and the skeptics of C, S and L searched the run's transcripts for the text. The script cannot see the branch, so it passes the text whenever the worker returned one. The line says that where the branch carries the file, the file is the report and this is its copy; where it does not, the text is the report, and the checks of `REPORT.md` are checks of it. It costs the rep
ort's size on every first and second skeptic, 27 to 59 KB in batch 7b, and duplicates the file where the write went through. `recordText` stays out: the skeptic reads `record.md` for check 8 only, and the gather writes it from the journal.

The skeptic refuses only for the change or the test; a citation, a wording or a cross-reference is a required correction (post-mortem 2026-09-29). So is a `testIsStage` rung's report whose diff is not the diff of the landed and post-edit tables: only a post-edit table the worker's transcript does not show written on the head's code is refused (until 2026-10-02, one the skeptic could not reproduce 
by its own run), and the worker's step 10 says a missing or wrong provenance line is corrected, not refused (`postmortem-2026-09-29/script-review.md`, finding 7). Check 2's provenance lines are such corrections since then, and the skeptic's own programs and their outputs stay under the worktree's `tmp/<slug>/skeptic/`, quoted in `SKEPTIC.md`, which it commits alone. Since 2026-10-03 it refuses onl
y where the repair touches code (climb batch 9's review, finding 1): a home owed that needs no code (a home-2 or home-3 test, a ledger row, a sentence of text) is a required correction with its row in `recommendedRows`, which the gather writes and opens, and a departure the batch record reserves as a reversible stop is a `stopsMet` entry, even where it departs from a decision on record (check 12 s
ays so too). Rung W of climb batch 9 was refused for three departures from the instance rule with no home, none needing code; its judge, repair and second skeptic cost 0.73M for tests and text of the kind the same batch's gather wrote for rows 597, 598, 602 and 609, about 0.2M (`reviews/batch-9-review.md`, section 3).

A judge's first ruling on a rung or on the merged tree runs on Opus; a second ruling on the same rung or tree runs on Fable (`judgeTier`; POSITIONS 2026-09-26). Its first item to read is the `checks` sub-list of the rung's briefing, or on the merged tree every rung's.

## Gather

Rungs are applied in ascending order of lowest edited line in the shared files, and a cited `file:line` that an earlier applied rung shifted is re-anchored by symbol (item 5). That rule is the records' (`REPORT.md`, `record.md` and the lines folded from them), not the tests'. Since the one-time strip of line numbers (`dc0eee2fe`), the tests cite the specification by section, and no stage re-anchor
s a test's citation. Each `recommendedRows` entry is opened or refused in one sentence (item 1). Since 2026-10-03 step 3 also corrects each sentence of the specification that a rung's `REPORT.md` lists as made false by its change, and each Appendix I Effect or note on walk or the compiled path that the gather's own record shows false: to what the code does, each clause checked against the code lin
e it states, in that rung's commit; such a sentence states what the code does and is not a text mismatch of step 5 (climb batch 8's review, finding 6, its gather's half; climb batch 9's, finding 3). Batch 8's gather saw rung Q's Effect false and let it stand, and in batch 9 no stage saw the one rung K made false; each took the review's judge and a repair, 0.53M and 0.39M (`reviews/batch-8-review.m
d`, section 5; `reviews/batch-9-review.md`, section 6). Since 2026-10-02 a skeptic's `skepticText` is the word `committed` once its `SKEPTIC.md` is committed, and its text only when the harness refused the write. That left one case no command covered: a first skeptic that committed its file and a second whose write was refused, where the branch carries the file, so its command is not run, and the 
second judgement was lost. For such a rung (two rounds, the second's `skepticText` a text) the script adds a command, "SKEPTIC.md, when the branch carries it", which leaves a file that opens with "# Second judgement" as it is and otherwise puts the second judgement from the journal above the file's text, under that heading and "## First round"; the gather runs it where the branch carries the file,
 and the plain command where it does not. It holds no double quote or backslash, since the gather reads it inside JSON; it was run on a scratch tree with a stand-in journal, the gap case, again on its own output (unchanged) and on a file the second skeptic had committed (unchanged). After a rung's patch is applied, each of its `REPORT.md`, `record.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` that the branch does not carr
y is written from `reportText`, `recordText` and `skepticText` verbatim (with a first skeptic round's text under "## First round" where there were two), since 2026-09-29 by one command per file that reads the field from the run's journal, `tools/journal-text.py`, which the script renders per rung in `textCommands`; a file the branch carries stands. The same holds for a rung that did not land, whos
e files are taken out of its branch. Files are staged by an explicit list and `git diff --cached --stat` is read before the commit, never `git add` of a directory (the protocol's hard rule on worker commits, 2026-09-19). A commit touching any path outside `explorations/` carries a `historical:` line (item 8, 7c). A rung that stopped, was dropped or was withheld by `landsOnlyWith` has its `SKEPTIC.
md` findings and its recommended rows — its files taken out of its branch path by path — folded under a "Not landed" heading with no source applied (7a, gap 3). Since the post-mortem of 2026-09-29 a landed rung's commit carries its `REPORT.md`, `SKEPTIC.md`, `JUDGE.md` and a specification rung's `decision-record.md`, and nothing else of its folder: `record.md` is folded, not landed; the gather
 writes the batch's `RECORD.md` once; and the tracked-path check that ran after the last commit (7b) went with the captures.

Step 5, added 2026-09-27, is measure 4 of `explorations/reviews/worker-global-decisions.md`: a judge's "For Pavol" section or a rung's list for him stopped in the rung's files and no stage moved it into `PLAN.md`'s queue (batch 5's judge on a size's range, rung F's `=` on `Number`, rows 417, 419 and 420). The script numbers every item a rung's worker, skeptic or judge returns in `forPavol` (`O.wor
ker.1`, `O.skeptic2.1`, `O.judge-stop.1`; `JUDGE_SCHEMA`'s `forPavol` is a list since then) and hands the gather the list. Each item becomes an entry of `PLAN.md`, under "Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed" when it asks for his decision or answer before work on the path can go on, in the group of the phase it must come before, else under "Off the path, parked", in the commit of its rung
 (a rung that did not land: the commit that carries its "Not landed" section). The gather's result lists each id with its section and entry in `pavolItems`, and each it could not put in, with the reason, in `pavolUnrouted`. The merged-diff review's check 9 (11 until the post-mortem of 2026-09-29, when its checks 8 and 9 left it) checks those entries and puts in any the gather missed, and its own i
tems (`review.1`); the repair on the merged tree puts in its judge's (`judge-review.1`, `judge-gate.1`). Nothing waits on them (Pavol, 2026-09-27): before the commit stage the script logs every id no stage put into `PLAN.md` under one of the two sections, with the gather's reasons, and every return of the script carries the items with `inPlan`, as `forPavol`, for the coordinator.

## Review beside the gate

Both run in one `parallel()` — the substitute the review recommended for the rejected rung chains, 14.7 minutes per batch off the serial tail. The risk of two agents committing at once is closed by the gate committing nothing; the commit stage adds its summary. The review records the head before and after its corrections commit, runs `git diff --name-only` between them, and returns every path ou
tside `explorations/`; a non-empty list re-runs the gate when no repair follows, and since 2026-10-02 only for a path the gate reads ("A repair of tests and records only", below). Its check 3, the folded record, takes the skeptic's check 8 since the same day: every rung's `FACTS` line true, sourced and checkable, every ledger note citing the row it names. A blocking finding that touches source, li
brary, checker, interpreter or specification goes to the judge, who orders a repair, after which the gate runs again when the repair changed a path it reads (`ProjectFortress/`, `Library/`, `build.xml`; since 2026-10-02, "A repair of tests and records only", below); a finding settled by tests and records only is routed by the review itself to the next batch and listed for Pavol, with no judge (pos
t-mortem 2026-09-29, section 2(b)); the review puts each routed finding into `PLAN.md` as `review-routed.N` in its corrections commit (`postmortem-2026-09-29/script-review.md`, finding 5). The review's own corrections stay inside `explorations/`: one that needs any other path goes in `blockingCode` or `routed` (`postmortem-2026-09-29/script-review.md`, finding 6). A review that returns nothing aft
er its three attempts holds nothing: the batch lands on its gate, and the result lists `review-missing.1` for the landing report (`postmortem-2026-09-29/script-review.md`, finding 12). The checker count, its check 9 until then, is the post-batch review's since the same date, so the review does not wait on the gate's table; its checks 10 and 11 are 8 and 9 since, and its tracked-path check 8 is gon
e. Check 8, added 2026-09-26 as check 10, lists in `stopsMet` every reserved stop a landed rung meets, in its hunks or where its records say so; it is not a blocking finding, and the commit stage reads it.

Check 9, added 2026-09-27 as check 11 with the gather's step 5, is the second check on the items for Pavol: each id's entry is in `PLAN.md` under one of the two sections and says what the item says, a missing or misplaced one the review puts in itself in its corrections commit, and its own points go in `forPavol` and into `PLAN.md` the same way; `pavolItems` lists what it put in. It is not a block
ing finding.

## Gate

Disk, `compileAll`, the library rebuild **plus a copy of the fresh library cache** for the ladder stage, `testFast`, `testSystem`, the summary and its comparison, the four-thread `atomic` runs, the ladder regression, since 2026-09-22 the checker count, and since 2026-09-27 the distance stage, started in the background right after `compileAll` and read last, as step 9; the last two have their own s
ections below. Logs go to `tmp/gate-batch-<N>/`, which `.gitignore:64` now ignores (appended at the end of the file so that no existing `.gitignore` citation moves), never committed. The `"Tests expected to pass are failing"` grep is gone (item 4): it is ant's own `<fail message=…>` and reads the same dial as `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`.

`summary.txt` comes from a fixed shell snippet in the script, not agent prose (item 3): one row per suite — `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped — read from the plain-formatter files under `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-*/` and `system-*/`, because the four parallel `testFast` tracks interleave their `Running` and `Tests run:` lines in the ant log and cannot be paired there; the
 `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` and `Total time` lines come from the logs. `gate_compare` diffs it against the newest landed summary, found with `git log --name-only`; a suite whose count fell, or that is gone, is red and named (gap 1). The `system-<i>` rows are compared by their sum, not one by one: `testSystem` is one suite sharded by sorted index (`FileTests.java:790-806`), so a file added to `ProjectFortr
ess/tests/` moves every later file along the shards; climb batch 2's gate went red on exactly this after `02d09a39f` added two interpreter tests between the baseline and the batch base (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/JUDGE-gate.md`). `run_bg` runs its command string in a subshell so a `cd` inside it cannot escape the log, and `atomic_runs` resolves its out-file before its own `cd` (both measured by
 that batch's gate stage). The first landed summary is `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/summary.txt`.

The four-thread stage runs the thirteen `atomic` programs the repair batch measured — the ten of `other_compiler_tests/atomicTest.test` plus `AtomicTopLevelObjectVar`, `AtomicTopLevelVar` and `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop` — three times each at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`. Any `FAIL`, `NO-PASS` or compile failure is red; a timeout is re-run once and then red. The 39 lines go into the summary.

The ladder stage re-runs the 85 files of `baseline-2026-09-19/pass-list.txt` and the eighteen microGPT components of `microgpt-phase.md` with the baseline's own drivers, copying the gate's fresh library cache instead of rebuilding one. The 85 are compared on phase **and** stdout, with a filter masking the `Operation took …ms` line: those three `nestedTransactions` captures are the only ones of t
he 85 whose output varies, and masking the line rather than exempting the file keeps the rest of their output checked. The eighteen are **compiled only** — `fortress compile`, the phase reached — never linked and never run in this stage (Pavol, 2026-09-19); when they one day compile, running them is a separate non-gating stage, not the gate. A `DOWN`, `STDOUT` or `MISSING` line is red unless `
expectedMoves` declared it; a move up is the batch's result and is reported. The judge's `gate` question now names the ways the gate can be red — five since the checker count below — and where each one's evidence is.

- **Appendix I's small items.** `TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]` in the api and the component, its five restated members kept, so that it gets back `MIN` and `MAX` (row 461 closed; built; taken on the coordinator's recommendation, and he wants it explained in more detail when he has the energy, "I need to pay that down", so it is on the list for his review).

### How we work

- **Test first, the test kept.** Every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus: the worker writes the test first, verifies that it actually fails, makes the fix, proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on; the full suite stays green. The unacceptable process is the one-off validation script, proving once by hand that the interpreter and the compiler agree and leaving no permanent check. The batches fix the issues the explorations captured as ledger rows, each with how to reproduce it, "Those are like our bug reports": the worker first commits the reproduction into the test suite, "this is how I have reproduced what the previous probe has discovered", then makes the fix, and the test passing demonstrates that the issue is fixed; "There isn't much more to it." The test captures the essence of the problem, not the shape the probe met it in, "do not blindly transpose the issue from the probe like think about it what's the core problem and capture that", written as a clean minimal version. Whether the test was seen failing first is read from the worker's transcript, not shown by a committed capture. The skeptic checks it there and runs no build to repeat it: "It should just check that the procedure of test first was followed. Not that it should be repeating the whole process, that is a fucking waste." Whether the suite runs per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per batch is in line with the rule. Every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test.
- **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test passes or fails, as the team designed the suite, and a value that matters is asserted in the test with the mechanisms the suite already has (an `assert` in an interpreter test, `run_out_equals` in a compiled one): "what is the purpose of a test suit that you just cannot run it and get a green? If everything that's encoded in it is, is okay and it turns red if it's not, why would you have to compare some values that it outputs? Those values must be part of the test." What a test prints beyond its checks does not matter: "When the designers of the test suite decided that it passes without any additional check, it is not needed to control its outputs." So no batch compares the corpus's printed outputs, no baseline is run to compare against, and no expected-output files are added to the interpreter suite, which has none; none of it is offered to him again.
- **Nothing is built or run twice on the same code.** "We don't want to re be rebuilding stuff that doesn't need to be rebuilt." The design, agreed with him and built into the batch script: the old code, the batch's base, is built once per batch, by the coordinator, before the launch, in a worktree nobody compiles or runs in (the script's `args.baseBuild`); "We just mechanically take the latest build and share it between each rung from the same baseline": every rung worktree is seeded from that one build in seconds (`coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean (his "Duh!" to "seeding a worktree by copying a built tree rather than rebuilding it"); the worker builds only what its own edit changed; the skeptic builds nothing, "very smart skeptics that just like reuse everything that was built during the rank phase as much as possible and just do their independent checks": it reads test-first from the worker's transcript, runs its own small programs on the new code with the rung's build and on the old code against the batch's one base build, through the rung's private seeded copy of it so that no two agents compile into one cache; the second skeptic checks only the repair against its own refusal; no stage re-runs a build, a suite or a measurement on a code state another stage has already run, and no agent reads again a log of output that has not changed: "I want to eliminate all waste of this type. Where we are re-executing stuff for no reason." How a worktree is seeded and what a worker clears after an edit or a failed build is engineering, measured before it is bu
- **The coordinator watches what it launches.** Only a long or large run the coordinator launches outside a batch, a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour or more, is watched against the estimate it was launched with, so that none runs away as probe P1 did (`coordinator/process-engineering/p1-cost.md`); when it passes its estimate the coordinator reacts, by an instruction to the worker or a stop, and its brief carries what keeps it efficient, a wait polled under the prompt cache's life among it. Ordinary workers carry no such procedure, and no ask is added before a probe: "I don't want you to become paranoid about running probes"; "I don't want the cargo cult of ... monitoring here. Only longer runs. ... I don't want you to burden with ... procedure on each call to workers." P1's waste was one the worker knew how to avoid: "an instruction to that worker would have corrected it."
- **A deeper pass, not a halt.** When something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch, no bisection of commits: "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle, no stop: "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one." What reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.
- **Forks are probed before a batch is briefed.** "if there are known decision forks, which we can evaluate using probes, we should be doing these during this phase, during this planning phase": a fork a probe can settle is probed first, so that the decision is his and the worker gets a clean task, never a decision left to a worker and reviewed after the fact. Rows are taken one per message with refreshers (other languages, what makes sense in a high-performance language), not in groups.
- **A brief describes the problem, not the solution.** "How do we prevent the myopic view? … I want to have full creativity of solutions": a worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language and the library offer before a design choice reaches him; a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the library gets around it (protocol principle 2). A worker that records timings records the CPU too, so that comparisons can be guessed at.
- **The mission briefing.** "this whole exercise is about in-context learning. You were not pre-trained on Fortress. And the language was not finished." The planner, who has the whole map, gives each rung a mission briefing from the map that its agents read in their first turn; the share of agents that use it is reported with each landing (it was about 80% once and fell to 25-35%: "We need to get back to that level"). The briefing is in neutral words, "the decisions on record" ("I am trying to stay humble and I don't want to see my name in there multiple times. Make this neutral."); the worker answers no required questions about its search ("I disagree with the procedural enforcement here ... it's giving the agent side quests that it's graded on instead of something that it should just take into consideration during the implementation"; the briefing says "this is not a Java, this is not a Scala, you are in unfamiliar territory", and then the worker "should focus on its tasks"); the skeptic checks the result against the library's way, the ledger and sibling sites, and the decisions on record.
- **No re-measuring what the record holds.** "you are wasting resources on remeasuring." A brief hands over what the record has measured as findings to cite and names the one new thing to measure; a clean worker is clean of our options, not of our measurements (protocol principle 5). A rung whose test is the checker-count or distance stage takes the last landed gate's tables as its before and does not re-run the stage on an unchanged base; the gate commits its per-site list so that the before is complete. The nine steps are a way to brief him on unfamiliar ground, a type-theoretical question answered from the theory, the rule and a few declarations; and one global rule is sought from type theory and the peers' implementations rather than a rule slapped on a rule ("I cannot be trusted to derive a rule that wouldn't break the whole system and be a hodgepodge of edge cases").
- **Reversible stops do not hold a batch.** A stop a batch record reserves for him (a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, an interpreter output a rung cannot account for): "These don't need me now. They are reversible things I can review later. Don't block start of next batches on these." It lands, the push and the next batch go ahead, and it is listed for his review (the protocol's first hard rule). An output difference the untouched tree already shows from run to run, the test's verdict unchanged, is not a stop but a ledger row ("we had a rule too stringent because the spirit of the test is still held"); a rung's small items go to the ledger for review, not to him one per message.
- **A blocking second review does not hold a green batch.** "we have enough rigor or robustness and backup in our processes after that, so that small failure in a rule should not be blocking ... landing large ships like this." After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green: the batch lands, the review's remaining findings go to the next batch and are listed for his review, and the post-batch review follows. A red gate after its repair still stops a batch. Built into `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual. The merged-diff review itself stays inside the batch, once, beside the gate, as the check of the merged tree's records, the stops and the routing before the push; removing it and moving its checks to the review after the batch is not taken (Fable's review of the batch practice against the Opus review's; he sided with Fable).
- **A tests-only repair does not rerun the gate.** "we are being overly pedantic for no good reason with like how the gates are set up ... we have to be weighing costs and benefits and we are not skipping the test, we are adding the test, we are moving stuff to following batches, we are running reviews after the fact, so we will catch stuff that the rerunning of a gate is not." A repair after the gate that changes no source, library, checker, interpreter or specification file runs its new tests in the harness on the merged tree; the first gate's tables stand; the landing records the new tests beside them; a repair that changes code reruns the gate. The same weighing of cost against what a rule protects applies to every rule of the batch workflow. Built.
- **What a batch commits.** "the commit discipline in a branch should not be different from what you will be committing to the main. Like don't keep temporary shit around. We are backing up the transcripts anyway from all the workers. So if we need to dig up something, how the worker arrived at some point, we have the full transcripts." A worker commits, on its own branch as on `main`, only what `main` is to hold: the Fortress change, its tests, its report, the lines for the ledger, FACTS and the plan, and a script or tool that is reusable ("If that script that batch contributes a script that is reusable, it goes in there", such as the documented way of running the checker as a shadow); no captured outputs, logs, raw outputs, script copies or other scratch are committed anywhere; new issues go to the ledger, reports into the batch's report; the process, and whether a worker wrote its test first and saw it fail, is read from the workers' transcripts, which the backup keeps. Deleting the `wip/` branches after a gate is his own chore in the GitHub web page, and he is not reminded of it. Built into the script, its manual and the protocol.
- **Workers commit their own files as they go.** "Workers should be committing themselves as they go, focused their files only. Protects against container failures and stops from harness bothering you about uncommitted files." They push to their own `wip/` branches as they work; the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the coordinator pushes `main` every few minutes ("I hope we are committing as we go because I worry that the container will get reset"). A protocol hard rule.
- **Which tier runs what.** "You can spend as much Opus workers as you want." The highest-risk decisions touch all three of specification, interpreter and compiler, which may disagree, and the design intent has to be inferred from the breadcrumbs left in all of them; the cheaper tier gathers the evidence into a condensed brief, and the high-level judgement of what makes sense given all the signals and what design balance lets the project grow belongs to the top tier, because that is the work it is for. Workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof"; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls". Sonnet is the tier for archaeology. Two workers launched on the wrong tier once cost him 1.7 million tokens "down the drain". The coordinating session runs on Opus, so that Fable's own weekly pool is kept "for more important work"; it moves to Fable at his word when the pool on all models is spent, and how the Opus trial is judged is in `coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-27-record-keeping.md`.
- **The judge's rulings.** A judge's first ruling on a rung or on the merged tree runs on Opus; a second ruling on the same rung or tree runs on Fable ("Second ruling is for Fable."), named in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` (`judgeTier`), so Fable is spent only when a second ruling happens. The review's judge rules while the gate runs on, and the gate writes its outputs under `tmp/` until the commit stage. A second repair round is not taken; option (b), approvals with required corrections when the fix is already written, has not been put to him (parked, `PLAN.md`).
- **The Fable rule.** "whenever it touches those three aspects of uh, library specification and implementation we are running the fable so if you use it sparingly I can pre-approve every such decision." The coordinator runs a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, for a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and the record has been searched and does not already settle it; he learns of it when the judgement is put to him in the ask form. He is asked first for any other Fable worker: a question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice, one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants Fable and Opus working independently. The standing pre-approvals: a judge's second ruling, and the top-tier reviews of the batch records.
- **One review after every batch.** "run the conformance review after every batch", combined with the process review into one pass, since "the amortized cost here is well worth the benefit": one Opus reviewer, reading only, does the conformance review, the process measures against `reviews/process-review-6b-7-7R.md` (misses by kind, those of items in the rung's own briefing, map use, briefing cost, re-measuring) and the routing check; the coordinator files what it finds in `PLAN.md` at the landing.
- **The phase-3 batches run on a standing go.** "I think you just carry on running the sequence of batches, I'll do the reset when I do it, If it stalls for a bit, I hope we'll recover without interruption. No need to complicate our runs with synchronization." And: "these are pre-approved. I want you to do autonomous overnight run." Each batch launches when the one before it has landed and its record is ready with no question open for him; a question a record raises goes to him first, except overnight, when it takes its recommended default and is listed for his review unless the default would reverse a decision of his, in which case that batch waits and the repair batch takes the slot; a run stalled by the limits is resumed with `resumeFromRunId`. A top-tier review in place of each coming batch record, in the form of `coordinator/climb-batch-7-review.md`, needs no further ask. The order is `PLAN.md`'s: batch 8 next. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run needs his explicit go, which for phase 3 this standing go is.
- **The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.** The practice after the post-mortem of the batch practice: the synthesis of its two reviews and both archaeologies, written into the script, its manual and the protocol, the script reviewed, a batch record rewritten to it and run on it, the landed batches' committed scratch cleaned in parallel, all built; of the post-mortem's four remaining questions, the output comparison is settled by his own position ("The suite's verdict is the check."), the merged-diff review stays by his word ("A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), new tests are named by topic, as he asked of the files named after batches, and the cleaning ran by kind on his rule that only the reports and the changes to the repository stay; the rest of the review loops inside a batch (no second review, a judge and a repair only for a finding in code) are the synthesis's defaults, in force. "You can now redeem yourself by fixing this and, and, and showing me that you can be token efficient and not do bullshit jobs that you invented yourself." Every step spends the fewest workers the step needs and measures nothing the record already holds.
- **The gate's comparisons.** A comparison masks Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions, with every masked difference listed for him; the `testSystem` comparison is the sum of the four shards; a name comparison, red when a test that passed before is missing or failing, is a script change put to him on its own (parked, `PLAN.md`); row 366 waits; no route C entry goes into Proposed Features. A team test line the flat tower breaks is respelled keeping the value the test checks, no assertion deleted, every such line listed for him with its before and after.
- **Estimates in the project's units.** Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run). "I'm on a max plan. Talk to me in tokens." Costs are given in tokens, never in dollars, and a token count counts writes only, cache writes and new input: "Token counts, always report only writes. Cached reads are de-facto free vis-a-vis writes."
- **Check-ins and stops.** A series of check-ins is spaced 45 minutes apart, since hourly ones risk "that this session KV cache is evicted and then the wake-up call pays the full" price; the one after a predicted process stop is a single extra. He sends messages at any time (a message during a turn is queued and kills nothing); he does not press stop while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; an accidental stop is said so, and the run is resumed, keeping every agent that had finished.
- **Where the work lives.** The work runs in the container on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it; transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded`, "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts?", and the lineages are joined at analysis time; the container recovery procedure is a lesson about the remote container (`coordinator/remote-container.md`), not a ledger row. Everything of ours is under `explorations/` ("to remove confusion for any workers"); the inventory note's own move list waits on his reading (parked, `PLAN.md`). Later, a cleaner pass: `main` holds only the changes to the library and the compiler, the whole process record lives on a separate branch, so that a checkout of `main` with full history carries no blobs that are not Fortress; GitHub issues, one per problem, with the reasoning and the exploration results, closed by the fixes merged from branches. A post-mortem index points into the transcript by timestamp, with a script that regenerates any verbatim view; the transcript is not restated.
- **The record is public and names models on purpose.** The protocol's rule against model identifiers is the harness's rule for what Claude itself writes and pushes, not a mandate to strip provenance from records that name models on purpose; "We are doing this work in public … there is no need to censor anything"; nothing in a transcript or an index is held back from the tree for that reason. The classifier refused writing this reading into the protocol itself, so it lives here.
- **The record's form: an optimized build and a debug build.** FACTS and POSITIONS are the optimized build, "what is true about the repository snapshot at this moment in time", written timelessly: no dates, no provenance, no account of what changed when or what corrected what; the history files are the debug build, with the full provenance, his quotes at their dates and every earlier text. "I don't want you to be searching with a flashlight in a dark room. I want to give you a map of the territory." A worker or a coordinator appending to FACTS or POSITIONS needs no timestamps; where one is written, or an entry corrects an earlier one, the next consolidation moves that provenance into the history and rewrites the fact or the position without it, at full informational fidelity. FACTS is consolidated before each batch launches, since workers read it and pay the cost. A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, pointing to the report or record that holds the detail, and the rung entries already in the file are shortened so, each earlier text verbatim in the history, before batch 8 launches: his choice of option 2 when the growth history showed the batches' rung entries, about 14 KB a landed batch, as most of FACTS' growth. The files read at every boot hold a clean current state and do not need edits as the work moves; the narrative of how a landed rung established a fact is history.
- **The statement for the public record on the usage limit.** "let the public record state that I'm now doing unpaid testing job of Anthropic's cloud infrastructure in my open source repository that is normally doing open source research of agentic coding capabilities." The account's weekly limit on all models stopped a running batch after its rung workers; later turns and subagents were served while the limit still read reached; he did not activate the promotional credit the panel offered, and his reading since is that visiting its page activated it unknowingly and that the work served was the $250 promotional credit for the cloud product, support having told him the offer had expired, "which was not true" (`coordinator/usage-metering-2026-09-30.md`, "After the report"); the container was booted afresh at each wake once nothing kept the session busy; at his word the batch was resumed to see whether it survives such interruptions and finishes.

## How he wants to be spoken to

- **The register.** "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations; replies very brief, plain English, no internal jargon. A wall of text is one he cannot absorb; the failure mode "is focused on over-compressing into a clever turn of phrase, but utterly fails in communicating clearly." Label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication).
- **Asks and decisions.** Decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat. An ask for a yes states, in the message itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs ("What are the consequences of the yeses? What does that work even want to do? ... this is just pressuring me to give approval without understanding"); one ask per message; no label stands in for an explanation, and a new name is defined in the sentence that uses it; the recommendation comes after the explanation, in one line, never instead of it.
- **Ownership.** "I need to maintain some ownership of this work, even if we are doing agentic coding … I did not know what you did. I need to know what you did. And I need to be aware of those choices and decisions because I am the one carrying the responsibility for the consequences as a director of this revival": every re-approval row is gone through in detail, grouped by theme, and the count of reversals is not the measure. A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
- **The coordinator's standing goal** is to model what Pavol already knows and where his context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the minimal set of relevant facts at the level he needs to decide; machine tokens are spent on thinking so that human context is protected. This came out of a compaction that left him "out of control, unaware of crucial details" while the coordinator was "taking unauthorized initiative which compounded my sense of helplessness to steer the Fortress revival efforts". The coordinator's two hats: "executive assistant here in this Fortress Revival project, helping me, the director, find a way forward, and the analyst that finds out what the fuck happened, why, and how do we move forward".

2	
3	# What a climb batch's agents spend their tokens on, by role
4	
5	Measured 2026-10-03 from batch 8 (21 agents, 7.72M, run `wf_603242ca-111`) and batch 9 (22 agents, 6.88M, run `wf_f747fd3e-9e4`). The totals agree with the two reviews' stage tables. Earlier measures this one adds to: `reviews/worker-context-cost.md` (gathering about a quarter of workers' cost, weighted by re-reads), `coordinator/skeptic-scope-judgement.md` (a skeptic's spend by check), `coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-29/characterization.md` (spend by stage), and the cost sections of `reviews/batch-8-review.md` and `batch-9-review.md`.
6	
7	## The answers
8	
9	Words used here. A **turn** is one call to the model. A call's **writes** are the tokens the cache had to store for it: what the agent's context grew by since the turn before (the model's own words, the tool results, the harness's one-line reminders), plus a full refill if the cache had expired. A **chain** is one rung's worker, skeptic, judge, repair and second skeptic. The **brief** is the first user message. The **briefing** is the record lookup (`facts-extract.sh`) the agents run in their first calls.
10	
11	**1. The fixed part is 19.5% of everything, 2.84M.**
12	
13	- Every agent starts with 69K to 108K tokens before it does anything (the first call's whole context; it wrote less of it where the cache already held the system prompt).
14	- The system prompt and tool schemas are about 36K. They are identical in all 43 agents. 19 first calls read them from a cache another agent had warmed (35.4K to 36.7K read). 24 first calls wrote them afresh: 0.87M.
15	- The harness's attachments (skill list, CLAUDE.md, deferred-tool names, environment) are about 6K, written by all 43: 0.26M.
16	- The brief is 27K to 56K, 1.70M in all (11.7%). By role: rung 29K, skeptic 44K, second skeptic 51K, judge 56K, repair 50K, gather 42K, gate 28K, merged-diff review 41K, the review's judge 28K, the review's repair 27K, commit 34K.
17	- The first 39.1K characters of every brief in batch 8 (42.6K in batch 9) are one shared prefix, the same in every agent of the batch. That is 16K to 18K tokens by the fit of first-call size on brief length (R2 0.99), or 11K at 3.6 characters a token. The rest of the brief is the role's text, the rung's tail (13K to 22K characters; it lists 28 to 37 briefing entries for a worker, 5 to 10 for a skeptic or judge, counted by their `positions:`, `spec:` and similar keys) or the worker's and skeptic's reports (the judge's brief carries them whole: 53K and 21K characters in batch 9's W).
18	- As a share of the agent's own writes the fixed part is: rung 8%, skeptic 19%, second skeptic 31%, judge 33%, repair 23%, gather 17%, review 19%, commit 50%, gate 59%, the review's judge 35% and repair 35%.
19	- Of the 2.84M, the identical-in-all-agents part (system and tools written afresh, attachments, shared prefix) is about 0.91M in batch 8 (11.8% of the batch) and 0.97M in batch 9 (14.0%). With 3.6 characters a token for the prefix: 0.79M and 0.83M.
20	
21	**2. The later calls: 11.76M, 80.5%.**
22	
23	- The agents' own thinking and narration, written back as input on the next turn: 3.92M, 26.9%. It is the largest single class. 4,644 turns, 845 tokens each on average (about 30 of them are the harness's reminder). Check: on the 26 turns whose output count is final, the inferred size matches the output count (median ratio 0.88).
24	- Tool results: 5.90M, 40.4%. The text of the calls themselves (commands, heredocs, edits, report files): 1.47M, 10.1%.
25	- One cache refill: 0.48M, 3.3%. 0.46M of it is rung M's single wait of 280 s in batch 8. Batch 9 had 13K.
26	- By what the calls were for, as a share of all writes:
27	  - the record and the specification 12.5% (the briefing 6.1%, the other record documents 4.5%, the specification 1.9%);
28	  - reports, records and transcripts of the chain's earlier agents 5.6%;
29	  - source, library and tests 7.8%;
30	  - search (grep, find, ls, git log) 4.9%;
31	  - git diff and show 5.1%;
32	  - edits to product and tests 1.7%, probes and scratch scripts 1.8%, report files and record edits 2.8%;
33	  - build, test and stage runs, probe runs and waits 4.3%, reading their output 2.6%;
34	  - git commit, push and the rest 0.9%, other 0.4%.
35	- Roles whose job is to check or judge (skeptic, second skeptic, judge, merged-diff review, the review's judge, gate) hold 6.26M, 42.9% of the writes. Rung workers hold 36.7%. The refusal cycle (judge, repair, second skeptic) is 3.34M, 22.9%, because both batches had two refusals.
36	
37	**3. Do they still explore on their own? A little, and mostly by searching.**
38	
39	- A rung worker's territory reading beyond what its brief names is 54K of its 536K (10%): 31K of searches that name no file, and 24K of reads of other files. The same for a skeptic is 23K of 321K (7%).
40	- Of the files a rung worker read that its brief did not name, 74% by tokens were named in the briefing it had read, in FACTS or INDEX, or in the maps. 26% (5.5K a worker) were on record nowhere, and some of those are the worker's own new test files read back.
41	- The briefs name most of what is read: 53% of a rung worker's territory-reading tokens go to files its brief names, 62% of a skeptic's. The rest is searching.
42	- No agent opened `INDEX.md`. FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX and the maps are read directly for 1.6K a rung (FACTS 0.9K, POSITIONS 0.1K, maps 0.6K). The record reaches the agents through the briefing, 6.1% of all writes.
43	- Before its first edit to a test or product file a rung worker has written 32% to 67% of its total (median 48% of the eight that finished): the first call, the briefing, the first reads and its probes. Batch 9's killed S was at 89%.
44	- Other roles, beyond the brief, K and share of their writes: second skeptic 13K (5%), judge 12K (5%), repair 17K (5%), gather 26K (5%), gate 8K (7%), review 10K (2%), the review's judge 27K (13%, the workflow script it read to see what the review may fix), the review's repair 9K (4%), commit 11K (7%). Almost all of it is search.
45	
46	**4. What several agents read alike: 29% of all reading.**
47	
48	- Of 4.73M tokens read (record, specification, source, library, tests, reports, diffs, searches), 1.39M were lines an earlier agent of the same batch had already been given.
49	- The followers in a chain (skeptic, judge, repair, second skeptic) read 1.77M, of which 750K (42%) the chain's earlier agents had read: the briefing slice 190K, git diff 142K, source 88K, reports 76K, specification 63K, library 60K, record documents 56K.
50	- The tail agents (gather, gate, review, the review's judge and repair, commit) read 1.28M, of which 398K (31%) earlier agents had read: git diff 122K, briefing 84K, reports 80K, specification 36K.
51	- What a brief carries is almost never read again: 1% to 4% of an agent's read tokens are text its own brief already held.
52	- The detail is in "Shared and repeated reading" below.
53	
54	**5. Re-reads within one agent are small: 4.4%.**
55	
56	- 249K of the 5.63M result tokens are lines the same agent had already been given, plus 31K read back from its own writes. Per role 1% to 7%. Re-runs of tests, probes and polls repeat 12% to 14% of their output, which is natural.
57	- The one clear case: the read-back of `SKEPTIC.md` in batch 8 (two first skeptics and one second skeptic, 8K to 10K each; none in batch 9).
58	- A file read in two or more calls is common (75% of file-read tokens), but that is a large file read in ranges, not the same text twice.
59	
60	**Is checking and re-checking all of it?** No. In the sense of tokens written:
61	
62	- 19.5% is the fixed part and 3.3% the one refill. Neither is checking.
63	- 26.9% is the agents' own thinking, in checking roles and building roles alike. Whether it was needed is not something this measure can say.
64	- 43% of the writes are in roles whose job is to check or judge, but inside them the same four things dominate: the fixed part (19% to 59%), thinking (12% to 32%), reading (the diff, specification, source, ledger) and the agent's probes.
65	- The part that is plainly not the job: identical text written again by each agent (about 0.9M a batch), a chain's followers re-reading the briefing and the diff (about 0.17M a batch), the review loop for one sentence (0.4M a batch, both batches), and in batch 8 the refill.
66	
67	Against the earlier measures:
68	
69	- Reading to learn or to verify (the record, specification, code, reports, diffs, searches) is 36% of all writes and 35% of a rung worker's (186K of 536K). `reviews/worker-context-cost.md` found a quarter of cost for rungs, skeptics and repairs, weighted by how often each result is re-read from the cache. This measure counts what is written, so the fixed part and the agents' own thinking, which that one left out of "gathering", show as the two largest classes.
70	- By stage, `characterization.md` had rung workers at 48.7% of output plus cache writes over 15 batches and the refusal cycle at 12.9%. In these two batches rung workers are 36.7% and the refusal cycle 22.9%, because both batches refused two rungs.
71	- The skeptic's totals and the opening quarter match `coordinator/skeptic-scope-judgement.md`. The reviews' stage tables match to the thousand.
72	
73	## Method
74	
75	- **Source.** The 43 agent transcripts under `/root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/subagents/workflows/<run>/`, labelled by `journal.jsonl`. They include the two rung workers batch 9 lost to the VM restart (W and S, first attempts) and their resumed attempts.
76	- **Writes** per turn are `cache_creation_input_tokens` plus `input_tokens`, one count per message id. They sum to the reviews' totals (7.72M, 6.88M).
77	- **Attribution.** For a turn, new content is the context size minus the previous turn's. It is the previous turn's output, its tool results and the reminders. A refill is the part of a turn's writes above that. A result is estimated at 0.40 tokens per character plus 110 per result (a fit on 55 clean turns gave 0.41 per character, R2 0.98; the earlier measure had 0.41 per byte and about 110 per call). A call's own text is 0.40 per character. What is left of the new content is the model's thinking and narration. Tool results are charged to the call that issued them.
78	- **Classes.** Each Bash command was split into simple commands and classed by its verb and the paths it names, in this order: build, test and stage runs, probe runs, waits, commit, writes (heredoc, redirect, `sed -i`, a Python writer), other git, then reads (by the kind of path: briefing, FACTS, POSITIONS, PLAN, ledger, INDEX and maps, batch record, specification, the chain's reports, source, library, tests, logs). A grep or find with no file operand is a search. A command that does several things is classed by the first of these it does. Of 36 calls over 1.5K tokens picked at random and checked by eye, 32 were in the right class; the four doubtful ones were a transcript query classed as search, two reads of harness scripts classed as output, and a script run classed as a library read. Treat class shares as good to a few points.
79	- **Beyond the brief.** A file read is "named in the brief" when its name or stem appears in the agent's first message; "in the briefing" when it appears in the briefing text the agent read; "on record" when it appears in FACTS or INDEX (or the maps) at the batch's base commit (`493b4076f`, `fa14a190c`). The test is lenient: a stem of six letters or more matches as a word.
80	- **Shared reading.** Lines of 25 characters or more in a result are matched with lines in earlier agents' results of the same batch (agents ordered by start time; the four rungs of a batch start together, so their mutual overlap is small by construction), and with the agent's own earlier results and calls for re-reads.

content.content:
## Shared and repeated reading

What was read by several agents of a batch, with tokens (lines of 25 characters or more matched across agents; the first reader's copy is not counted as repeated):

- **The briefing.** 833K read by 32 agents, 341K (41%) lines an earlier agent had already read. In a refused chain the follower slices are the same text: batch 8's Q slice (8.0K) was read by the skeptic, judge, repair and second skeptic (32K); O's (16.6K to 17.9K) by the same four (68K). In batch 9 the followers' slices were 65% to 98% lines of the worker's own briefing (R 94%, K 91%, W 89%, S 65%), and the skeptic, judge and repair of S each read 9.3K of the same text. Repeats within a chain: 69K (batch 8), 121K (batch 9).
- **Git diff and show.** 685K read, 284K repeated (41%): judge 90%, the review's judge 80%, review 41%, gather 47%, skeptic 41%.
- **Specification.** 257K, 117K repeated (45%). `changes.tex` 75K by 17 agents, `inference.tex` 40K by 13, `conversions-coercions.tex` 30K by 7.
- **Source, library, tests.** 1.04M read, 284K repeated (27%). `OverloadingChecker.scala` 92K by 10 agents (56K repeated), `EvaluatorBase.java` 71K by 6 (26K), `FortressLibrary.fsi` 67K by 21 (28K), `FortressLibrary.fss` 80K by 22 (18K), `OverloadedFunction.java` 60K by 9 (24K), `RangeInternals.fss` 66K by 7 (13K), `FileTests.java` 49K by 13 (15K).
- **The chain's reports.** `SKEPTIC.md` 144K by 18 agents (68K repeated), `REPORT.md` 141K by 14 (17K), `JUDGE.md` 62K by 9 (21K), `record.md` 57K by 8 (18K), `decision-record.md` 47K by 8 (14K). These are handovers already; the followers also read the primary text.
- **The record.** The ledger 163K by 31 agents (12K repeated, mostly different rows), PLAN 103K by 8 (the gather, the review, the review's repair), FACTS 55K by 9 (gather 11 reads, commit 8), `CLIMB-BATCH-8.md` 81K by 14 (49K repeated; batch 9's `CLIMB-BATCH-9.md` 30K by 7).
- **The fixed start.** System prompt and tools 36K, attachments 6K, shared prefix 16K to 18K: identical in all 43 first calls; see answer 1.
- **What the brief already carried.** 1% to 4% of read tokens in every role. The briefs carry the reports as structured results; the agents read the files and the primary text, not the same lines.

What of it could be done once:

- The fixed start, by the harness's cache (lever 1).
- The chain's briefing slice, computed once as the part not already in the worker's (lever 5).
- The review and the gather read the same reports and diffs (lever 7), but the review exists to check the gather.
- The followers' reading of the specification, source and diff is the checking itself. The lines are repeated, but an agent that does not look at them cannot check them. The 750K the followers read twice is the ceiling for that reading, not a saving.

## Levers

Savings are per batch, in tokens written, from the two batches. They overlap: lever 1 and lever 6 pull the same text in opposite directions. No recommendation.

1. **Put the identical start where the cache can share it.**
   - Saves: with the five-minute cache as it is, a cache break after the shared block would let the 9 to 10 agents a batch that already hit the system cache also hit the attachments and the shared prefix: 0.15M to 0.24M a batch (2% to 3%). With a longer life (one hour) or a keep-warm call, every first call after the first would read all of it: 0.74M to 0.91M a batch (10% to 13%), after one write of about 60K.
   - Evidence: 19 of 43 first calls read exactly 35.4K to 36.7K from cache, the system prompt and tools, and nothing after it, though 39K to 43K characters of prefix and the attachments were identical in every agent of the batch. Agents launched together or close behind another (the rungs, the first skeptics, part of the refusal chains) hit; the 24 that started with a cold cache (the first of each wave, all the tail agents) missed.
   - Cost or risk: it needs a harness feature (a cache break after a shared block, a longer life, or the shared text in the system prompt). I could not tell from the transcripts whether the workflow tool offers one. The shared block would have to come before anything per agent (the environment attachment, the rung). A one-hour write is priced higher per token than a five-minute write, so the saving in money is smaller than in tokens.
2. **Several reads in one turn.**
   - Saves: agents issue 1.03 calls a turn. 2,513 of the 4,644 turns (54%) are a read turn right after another read turn, and they carry 2.38M of the 3.92M thinking tokens (946 each, 1.19M a batch). If a quarter to a third were merged into the turn before, and a merged turn lost its separate thinking: 0.30M to 0.40M a batch (4% to 5%). Not counted: each turn avoided also avoids reading the whole context from the cache.
   - Evidence: the counts above; the shared prefix says nothing about issuing calls together.
   - Cost or risk: some reads depend on the one before (a grep, then a `sed` at the hit). An agent may over-fetch, which adds tokens. The saving assumes the thinking really goes; that is untested.
3. **The review fixes a text-only finding itself.**
   - Saves: 0.3M to 0.35M when it recurs. It recurred in both batches: the review's judge and repair wrote 0.41M and 0.39M for one sentence of `changes.tex` (batch 8 review section 5, batch 9 review section 6). My estimate for the review's own fix is 0.05M.
   - Evidence: the two reviews; 71K and 70K of each pair is the fixed part, and the repair's briefing reads 62K.
   - Cost or risk: in batch 9 the judge found two errors in the review's proposed sentence. A review that fixes alone has to do that clause-by-clause check itself, or a wrong sentence lands in the specification. The batch 8 review already listed this as its measure 6; the batch 9 review notes the review's prompt still lists the specification among the paths it may not fix (`climb-batch-workflow.js:1635`).
   - A narrower form: the review's repair runs the briefing slice for the finding's rung only. Saves 0.03M to 0.06M a batch (46K and 73K read, about 15K needed). Cost: it loses the cross-rung context for a finding that spans rungs.
4. **The gate runs as a script, with an agent only on failure.**
   - Saves: 0.12M (batch 9, one gate) to 0.24M (batch 8, two gates).
   - Evidence: 59% of a gate's writes are the fixed part (71K), 12% thinking, the rest runs and reading summaries. Both gates of batch 8 had the same brief.
   - Cost or risk: a script must print the landed tables and apply the pass rule. A flaky stage or a failure needs a model. The agent currently decides when a rerun is owed.
5. **Followers read the part of the briefing the worker had not.**
   - Saves: 0.07M to 0.12M a batch (69K in batch 8, 121K in batch 9).
   - Evidence: skeptic, judge, repair and second skeptic of one rung read the same slice; in batch 9 it was 65% to 98% lines of the worker's own briefing.
   - Cost or risk: the skeptic's slice exists for an independent check against the record; if it is mostly the worker's, that check is small. A tool change to diff the slice against the worker's list.
6. **Cut the shared prefix by role.**
   - Saves: 0.03M to 0.06M a batch. The worker sections (the three homes 4.8K characters, four rules 3.5K, what you write 3.1K, the briefing and the map 2.6K, 3.9K more of register, cite, commit and push, an existing branch and compaction, and in batch 9 4.5K about edits and the old code) are 18K to 22K characters, 4.5K to 9K tokens, in the prefix of the gate, commit, gather, review, the review's judge and repair: six or seven agents a batch.
   - Evidence: the prefix's section sizes in the two batches' briefs.
   - Cost or risk: several prefixes to keep in step; a role may need a rule that was cut. It works against lever 1, which wants one identical block.
7. **The gather leaves the review a digest.**
   - Saves: at most 0.07M a batch: the review re-reads 68K of lines earlier agents had read (reports 21K, git diff 34K), commit 6K.
   - Evidence: the repeated shares above (reports 39%, git diff 41%).
   - Cost or risk: the review exists to check the gather's fold; a digest from the gather weakens that. The high-risk lever.
8. **Anchors in the brief for the searches.**
   - Saves: up to 0.36M a batch is all of search (4.9%); the part that is locating a line in a file the record names is not separable in this data. If a fifth: 0.07M.
   - Evidence: a rung worker's searches are 26% of its territory reading, and 74% of the files it read beyond the brief were named in the briefing or the record, so the exploring happens inside known files.
   - Cost or risk: file and line ranges to add to each tail; stale after the first edit.

Already pulled between batch 8 and 9, visible in these numbers:

- The wait cap: the refill fell from 0.46M to 13K.
- The second skeptic narrowed to the repair: 0.69M to 0.40M for two.
- The skeptic's `SKEPTIC.md` read-back and the batch record reads: 4.7K and 7.6K to nothing and 1.7K a first skeptic.
- Seeded base builds: builds, stage runs and waits of a first skeptic 9.2K to 1.8K; of a rung worker 22K to 16K.

## Limits

- Class shares are estimates: a result's size is 0.40 tokens a character, the thinking is the remainder, and each command is classed by its verbs (about one call in ten is mixed).
- The first-call split between the system prompt, attachments and brief rests on a fit across the 43 first calls (42.5K fixed plus 0.42 tokens a character of brief, residual up to 3K). The brief's own density varies from 0.16 to 0.5 tokens a character by section, so the shared prefix is 11K to 18K tokens.
- "Named in the brief" is lenient (stems match); "not on record" includes the worker's own test files read back.
- The ordering behind "read by an earlier agent" is start time. The four rungs of a batch run together, so their overlap is understated. A line match misses a paragraph reflowed between two documents.
- The share of the thinking that was needed, and of the briefs' content that was used, is not measured. Only what was written, repeated and re-read.
- The killed batch 9 workers are in the rung averages (10 transcripts, not 8).

## Files

Session `fe616d40` scratchpad, `labor/`: `parse.py` (transcripts to turns, calls, results), `cls.py` and `cls2.py` (the command classifier), `acct.py` (writes per turn and per call), `tab1.py`, `gen_matrix.py`, `gen_agents.py` (the role matrix and the per-agent table), `topfiles.py` (top reads), `explore.py` (beyond the brief), `shared.py`, `reread.py`, `inbrief3.py` (shared reading, re-reads and brief overlap). Run `python3 parse.py && python3 acct.py` first.

Fortress revival · process engineering · 3 Oct 2026

Batch 10, designed blind

Two designers each wrote a workflow for climb batch 10 from its goals alone. Nothing they wrote was run. This page sets the two designs beside the pipeline batch 10 is running on now.

Reading the numbers

M is a million tokens written: cache writes plus new input, with cached reads not counted. That is the project's unit POSITIONS.

Each number carries a tag naming its file:

  • B9 §nexplorations/reviews/batch-9-review.md
  • Rec §nexplorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-10.md
  • Briefexplorations/coordinator/process-engineering/design-batch10-brief.md
  • Fable §n…/process-engineering/design-batch10-fable.md
  • Opus §n…/process-engineering/design-batch10-opus.md
  • Labor…/process-engineering/labor.md
  • Script :nexplorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js
  • Manualexplorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md
  • POSITIONSexplorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md
  • Heldexplorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md (the boot note)
  1. The question and what ran
  2. How the designers were briefed
  3. The pipeline batch 10 runs on
  4. The two designs
  5. Side by side, role by role
  6. Where the tokens go today
  7. Decisions put to you
  8. What comes next

1The question and what ran

  • The question. What workflow would a designer build for batch 10 from its goals alone, and where would it spend less than ours? In the brief's words: "to see what you would design from the goals alone" Brief.
  • What ran. Two design-only workers, one on Opus and one on Fable, each blind to our pipeline and to the other Held.
  • What each wrote. One document: the design, its Workflow script, how it checks correctness, its cost estimate, and what to measure or decide first Brief.
  • Nothing was built, run or tested. Both designs exist on paper only.
  • Batch 10 runs now on the existing pipeline, launched at 05:27 UTC Held, so its measured cost can be set beside both designs once it lands.

2How the designers were briefed

They got the goals, your binding rules, the machine's costs and a general scripting reference. They did not get our pipeline, but parts of it showed through.

What they were given

  • Batch 10's goals: the record's sections 1 to 5 Brief. These describe four rungs. A rung is one piece of work, done by one worker in its own copy of the tree. W changes walk's (the interpreter's) load-time checks; C repairs the compiled checker's defects; G and N repair one-off slips in two parts of the library Rec §1.
  • Your requirements from POSITIONS, as binding Brief:
    • test first, the test kept in the corpus;
    • the suite's verdict is the check, with no output comparisons;
    • nothing built or run twice on the same code;
    • both full suites green on the merged tree before anything lands (testFast, which holds the compiler tests, and testSystem, the interpreter tests);
    • workers commit only what main is to hold;
    • the specification revised with each change in the S1 form (a marked callout at the passage and an Appendix I entry with the reason);
    • tiers: Opus for workers, Sonnet for archaeology (reading history, transcripts and logs), Fable, the top tier with its own scarcer weekly pool, only for judgements;
    • costs in tokens written.
  • The machine's costs Brief: 4 CPUs; two agents at a time; about 45K tokens before an agent does anything; a prompt cache that lives 5 minutes, so a longer wait rewrites the agent's whole context; a built tree copied into a new worktree in about 3 s; the session stopped after about 13 hours; past batches wrote about 6M to 8M each.
  • The workflow-authoring skill, described next.

The workflow-authoring skill

  • It is a reference for writing Workflow scripts: how agents are started, chained and run in parallel, how a stopped run resumes, and the traps.
  • It also lists general quality patterns: several skeptics trying to refute a finding, a panel of judges, searching until a round finds nothing new, a last critic asking what is missing.
  • It says nothing about Fortress, this project or its pipeline.
  • It advises leaving each agent's tier unset. Both designs set a tier on every agent because the brief told them to.

Choices that came from the brief, not from the designers

  • The tiers: Opus for every worker and checker, Fable only for rulings, Sonnet only for archaeology. The Opus design uses Sonnet for a cost measurement. The Fable design stretches Sonnet to the gate and the landing, and asks you first Fable §5.
  • Test first, the test committed alone, and checked by reading the worker's transcript.
  • The two full suites run once on the merged tree before landing.
  • One base build before the launch, every worktree seeded from it in about 3 s Brief, and the old code run from that base build.
  • Every long wait polled in steps under 5 minutes, because of the cache: 270 s in the Fable design Fable §2, 260 s in the Opus design Opus §1.
  • The longest rung started first, because only two agents run at a time.
  • A run stopped at 13 hours is resumed from its journal.

What is left as the designers' own: how many checkers, when a ruling happens and on which tier, and what runs after the rungs.

How blind they were: partly

  • Withheld: the pipeline script, its manual, the record's sections 6 to 8, the batch reviews and the post-mortems Brief.
  • But section 1 of the record ends with "Cost": batch 9's cost by stage (workers 2.69M, first skeptics 1.24M, two refusal chains 1.40M, the tail 1.56M) and the old pipeline's estimate for batch 10, 6M to 7M Rec §1. Both designs measure their savings against these numbers.
  • Section 1 also defines a rung, the skeptic and the gate. Section 4 names the gather and the order it merges in.
  • Section 3's rung texts carry lines of the existing pipeline: each rung's "For the skeptic" paragraph and its gate lines. The brief said so and asked the designers to read them as the old way Brief.
  • POSITIONS describes parts of it: the shared base build and a skeptic that reads instead of rebuilding ("Nothing is built or run twice on the same code."), the merged-diff review beside the gate ("A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), and Opus for a judge's first ruling, Fable for a second ("The judge's rulings.") POSITIONS.
  • build-cache-exploration.md, which the brief pointed to, describes batch 8's skeptics, second skeptics and second gate.
  • The Opus designer declares a slip. The file viewer returned the record in two pages, and it read the second, sections 6 to 8. It marks what it took from them with [6-8]: the reuse of the base build, the briefings' sizes and the worker time guesses Opus header.

So both designers knew the pipeline's shape in part: worker, skeptic, one repair, merge, gate. The experiment shows best what each would change in that shape, not what each would invent from nothing.

3The pipeline batch 10 runs on

Nine roles, all Opus but a judge's second ruling. Batch 9 spent 6.88M on it B9 §7.

A rung's chain runs from its worker to its second skeptic. Everything after the rungs is called the tail. Tiers are set in Script :51–58. Each cost below is batch 9's measured spend B9 §7.

  1. Rung workerOpusone per rung

    Works in its own worktree (a copy of the tree on its own branch), seeded from the one base build. Writes the test, sees it fail, commits it alone, then makes the fix and its specification text, and pushes as it goes.

    Batch 9: 2.69M over 6 agents; about 2.2M without the VM restart B9 §7

  2. SkepticOpusone per rung

    Reads the worker's transcript to see the test failed first. Runs its own small programs on the new and the old code. Builds nothing. Approves or refuses. Since 3 Oct it refuses only when the fix needs code; a wording or record fix is a required correction that the gather makes Manual.

    Batch 9: 1.24M over 4 B9 §7

  3. JudgeOpusFable 2nd ruling

    Acts on a refusal, before any repair: it rules repair, drop or stop Script :2541–2552. A second ruling on the same rung runs on Fable.

    Batch 9: 0.45M over 2 B9 §7

  4. RepairOpus

    One round, in the rung's worktree, on the judge's ruling.

    Batch 9: 0.56M over 2 B9 §7

  5. Second skepticOpus

    Checks only the repair, against its own refusal.

    Batch 9: 0.40M over 2 B9 §7

  6. GatherOpus

    Puts each approved rung on main as one composed commit. Writes the ledger rows (the list of known defects), the FACTS and PLAN lines and the batch record.

    Batch 9: 0.47M B9 §7

  7. Merged-diff reviewOpus

    Runs beside the gate. Reads the merged diff and the records. A blocking finding in code gets its own judge and one repair.

    Batch 9: 0.42M, its judge 0.19M, its repair 0.20M B9 §7

  8. GateOpus

    Builds the merged tree once. Runs testFast, testSystem, the four-thread atomic runs, the compile ladder, and the two report-only stages: the checker count and the distance, two measures of what the compiled checker still refuses in the library Manual.

    Batch 9: 0.13M B9 §7

  9. CommitOpus

    Lands the gate's tables, pushes main, and starts the two microGPT runs under walk.

    Batch 9: 0.15M B9 §7

Batch 9, measured: 6.88M over 22 agents, 5 h 44 min. The tail: 1.56M B9 §7.

Batch 10 on this pipeline, the record's estimate: 6M to 7M, 14 to 18 agents, 6 to 9 hours Rec §1.

4The two designs

Both keep the shape: workers, a checker per rung or pair, one repair round, a merge, one gate. They differ in the checking and in the tail.

The Fable design

Before the launch the coordinator builds the base once, about 4 minutes, and puts each rung's section of the record into the run's arguments Fable §2. Order: C, W, N, G, two at a time Fable §1.

  1. WorkerOpus×4

    Its brief is its rung's section of the record, with no separate briefing. Tests first, committed alone. Then one suite run, chosen by what the edit can break: W runs testSystem; C runs the compiler and library tracks of testFast; G and N run only their own tests, which load the whole library. C, G and N run the two stages once at the end. It writes the ledger, FACTS and PLAN lines into its report, not into those files.

    Estimate: 2.5M to 3.3M Fable §4

  2. SkepticOpus×4

    Reads the git log, the diff, the report and the tool lines of the worker's transcript. Runs 3 to 6 programs of its own on new and old code. Builds nothing. It may refuse only on six listed grounds Fable §2:

    • a test not seen failing first, or not committed alone;
    • a stop of the brief met and not listed;
    • a fix against the text or library practice the brief cites;
    • a file touched outside the brief's list;
    • a value changed without the brief's warrant;
    • a test that cannot fail for the reason it names.

    Anything else is a note for you.

    Estimate: 0.8M to 1.2M, 0.2M to 0.3M each Fable §4

  3. After a refusalone chain expected
    • Opus Repair of exactly the named grounds: 0.3M.
    • Opus Second read, of those grounds only: 0.15M.
    • Opus Ruling, only if the second read refuses again, approve or drop: 0.15M.
    • Fable Second ruling, only if the Opus ruling says the dispute is a design question across two of the specification, the library and the implementation: 0.15M, rarely.

    A rung not approved stays on its branch; the batch lands without it.

    Estimate: 0.6M a chain; one expected, two budgeted Fable §4

  4. GatherOpus

    Merges the approved branches with merge commits in a seeded worktree, and writes the records from the workers' reports.

    Estimate: 0.25M Fable §4

  5. GateSonnet, low effort

    One build of the merged tree, then testFast, testSystem, the ladder, the count and the distance, one after another. A red gate gets one Opus repair and one more gate.

    Estimate: 0.10M to 0.15M; a red gate adds 0.4M and 0.1M, expected once in three batches Fable §4

  6. LandingSonnet, low effort

    Writes the gate's numbers into the landing note, fast-forwards main, pushes, starts the microGPT runs.

    Estimate: 0.08M Fable §4

Not in it: the merged-diff review, and a judge on every refusal Fable §1.

Estimate: about 5.2M (4.3M to 6.8M), including about 0.25M of the coordinator's own work outside the run. 11 to 19 agents, 13 to 14 expected. About 9 to 10 hours Fable §4.

The Opus design

Before the launch the coordinator builds or reuses the base build, renders each rung's briefing, and commits two small tools: gate.sh, the gate's steps as one script, and test-first-trace.py, which prints a worker's test runs from its transcript Opus §2, §5. Order: C, N, G, W, two at a time Opus §1.

  1. WorkerOpus×4

    Its rung's section plus its briefing. Tests first, committed alone; the fix; the text in the S1 form. One reach run, the part of the suite its change can reach: testFast for C, testSystem for W, N and G. C, N and G run the two stages once. New ledger rows get placeholders that the integrator numbers.

    Estimate: 2.25M (1.8M to 2.75M) Opus §4

  2. CheckerOpus×3

    One for W, one for C, and one for N and G together. Checks test first from git and the transcript, the paths touched, each fix against its text or precedent, at most eight programs of its own, the worker's results, and the revised text Opus §2. It may commit text-only corrections. It approves unless a code or test finding stands on a program or a cited line.

    Estimate: 0.88M (0.69M to 1.12M) Opus §4

  3. After a refusal1.4 expected
    • Opus Repair: accepts each finding, turning the checker's program into a test that fails first and then fixing it, or contests it with evidence. About 0.28M each, 0.43M expected.
    • Fable Ruling, only for a contested finding: one ruling, final. About 0.15M each, 0.05M expected.
    • Opus Second repair, only after an upheld ruling: 0.04M expected.

    No second skeptic.

    Estimates Opus §4

  4. IntegratorOpus

    Merges with merge commits into a fresh, unseeded worktree, numbers the rows, starts gate.sh in the background (a clean build and the full gate, 25 to 35 minutes Opus §2), and writes the records while it runs. Pushes a work branch, never main.

    Estimate: 0.28M Opus §4

  5. ReviewerOpusbeside the integrator

    Reads the four diffs side by side for what no single check could see. Its text corrections land before the push. Its code findings become rows for the next batch and block nothing.

    Estimate: 0.25M Opus §4

  6. Gate repairOpusred gate only

    Repairs the merged tree as a whole, then one more gate.

    Estimate: 0.1M expected (0.4M at a 0.25 chance) Opus §4

  7. LanderOpus, low effort

    Applies the review's text corrections, checks that no gated path changed since the gate, pushes main, starts the microGPT runs.

  8. MeasureSonnet, low effort

Batch 10, designed blind

Two designers each wrote a workflow for climb batch 10 from its goals alone. Nothing they wrote was run. This page sets the two designs beside the pipeline batch 10 is running on now.

Reading the numbers

M is a million tokens written: cache writes plus new input, with cached reads not counted. That is the project's unit POSITIONS.

Each number carries a tag naming its file:

  • B9 §nexplorations/reviews/batch-9-review.md
